| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/tasks/:id/merge-gate` | Read-only: merge readiness of every linked pull request |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/tasks/:id/merge-gate` | Retry the merge and close. Honors the close gate unless `respect_close_gate` is false |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/tasks/:id/complete` | Complete a task that is not close-gated, merging ready pull requests first |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/tasks/:id/close` | Close-gated close from the board. Merges, then closes |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/approvals/:id/close-approve` | Approve a close card. Merges, then closes. Refuses with 409 if any pull request of a task is not ready. All-or-nothing applies per task: a card covering several tasks runs them in sequence, so an earlier task may already be merged and closed when a later one fails |

### The merge-gate endpoint

`GET /cockpit/api/tasks/:id/merge-gate` returns the task's close-gate flag and one entry per pull request.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "task": { "status": "doing", "human_approval_to_close": true },
  "prs": [
    {
      "repo": "example/app",
      "number": 18,
      "merged": false,
      "ready": false,
      "reason": "checks_red",
      "checks": [{ "name": "build", "status": "completed", "conclusion": "failure" }]
    }
  ]
}
```

`POST` to the same path runs the merge and close. A close-gated task refuses it with `close_gated` unless the caller passes `respect_close_gate: false`, which the Approvals and Close buttons do because the person's click is the approval.

## Set up, repository, and revoke

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/integrations` | Connection status, without stored secrets |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/connect` | Start the GitHub connect. Body `{ "provider": "github" }`. Returns an `authorize_url` |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/revoke` | Disconnect. Body `{ "connectionId": "..." }`. Merging stops until you reconnect |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/pull-requests/check-in` | Queue a task to check in one repository. Body `{ "repo": "owner/name" }`. Repeating it returns the open task instead of making another |
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/pull-requests` | The pull request and branch list for the Pull requests view |

Revoking stops later reads and merges. Rows already imported, and pull requests already merged, stay.

## Chytr log drain

The log drain forwards agent session logs to an external viewer. It is separate from merging. Setup lives on [Integrations](/docs/features/integrations).

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/chytr` | Drain status, without secrets |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/chytr` | Save the base URL and keys, or turn the drain on or off |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/chytr/test` | Check that the stored key reaches the drain |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/chytr/backfill` | Ask the drain to push a page of history. Optional `batch_size`, `max_batches`, `repo`, `reset` |

## Permissions

Connecting, revoking, and the endpoints above use the signed-in session. Closing through an agent needs `tasks:write`. GitHub access is the workspace connection, not a scope on a token. Row access follows RLS: admins see all rows, members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `task_request_close` with the pull request URL. There is no merge tool.

```json
{
  "tool": "task_request_close",
  "arguments": {
    "task_ids": ["task-1"],
    "pr_url": "https://github.com/example/app/pull/18",
    "note": "Docs match the branch."
  }
}
```

Expected result, task not close-gated and the pull request ready: the pull request merges as a merge commit and the task is `done`. If the task is close-gated, the task moves to `review` and a close card waits for a person. If checks are red, nothing merges and the result gives the reason.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "status": "done"
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/cases

# Cases

## What it does

Cases keep a customer problem on the account it belongs to, so the outcome is something you can confirm instead of a note that disappears.

Open **Cases** (`/cases`). A case needs an account. A project is optional. You can open one from the board and mark it resolved. Outcomes are the committed results on a deal or a project. An agent can create and update an outcome. Setting it achieved files a human-only card (`engagement_outcome_achieve`). The agent cannot flip that itself.

The screen only calls the case routes. Agents use the case and outcome tools and see the same rows.

## MCP tools

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `cases_list` | `cases:read` | List. Filters: `status`, `account_id`, `project_id`, `limit` |
| `case_create` | `cases:write` | Open a case. `account_id` is required |
| `case_update` | `cases:write` | Update a case and link or unlink an outcome |
| `outcomes_list` | `engagement_outcomes:read` | List outcomes |
| `outcome_create` | `engagement_outcomes:write` | Create an outcome. Cannot set achieved |
| `outcome_update` | `engagement_outcomes:write` | Update fields. Does not confirm or achieve |
| `outcome_confirm` | `engagement_outcomes:write` | `confirm`, `reject`, or `achieve`. Achieved files a human-only card |

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/cases` | List or create. Create requires `title` and `account_id` |
| `GET`, `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/cases/:id` | Read or update, including status `resolved` |
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/cases/:id/outcomes` | Outcomes on the case |

List filters: `status`, `account_id`, `project_id`, `outcome_id`, and `q`.

## Permissions

Token scopes come from one permission-set layer. Case reads need `cases:read`. Case writes need `cases:write`. Outcomes use `engagement_outcomes:read` and `engagement_outcomes:write`. The screen uses the signed-in session.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `case_create` with the account the issue belongs to.

```json
{
  "tool": "case_create",
  "arguments": {
    "title": "Nightly load failed twice",
    "description": "The second run stopped on the same file.",
    "account_id": "account-1",
    "status": "open"
  }
}
```

Expected result: an open case on that account. `cases_list` with `status` `open` includes it. `outcome_confirm` with `action` `achieve` does not mark the outcome achieved. It files a pending card a person has to accept.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "title": "Nightly load failed twice",
  "status": "open"
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/agents

# Connecting agents

## What it does

Connecting agents gives each runtime a way to call chytr and a way for chytr to wake it, so work moves in both directions without sharing one secret.

An agent needs two different credentials if you want both directions:

| Credential | Direction | Where you create it |
|---|---|---|
| Personal access token (`cbpat_…`) | Agent calls chytr MCP | **Admin → API Keys** |
| Runtime webhook secret | chytr calls the agent | **Agents** (`/settings/agents`), stored in Vault |

A token is not a runtime, and a runtime secret is not a bearer token for MCP.

## MCP endpoint

```
POST https://chytr.example.com/api/mcp
Authorization: Bearer cbpat_…
```

The body is MCP JSON-RPC. The Next.js route proxies to the `mcp` Edge Function. `GET /api/mcp` does not serve the protocol. It responds with the metadata hint clients use for auth.

OAuth clients discover the resource at `GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`. The authorization server is your Supabase Auth issuer. Consent is served by the `auth-pages` function, not by the chytr login page.

An agent token carries the permission sets and extra scopes attached to that token. A signed-in user's API token is a separate case: it is meant to inherit that user's permission set, and that inheritance is still planned. Both are in [Permissions and API keys](/docs/reference/permissions). The tool catalog is in [MCP tools](/docs/reference/mcp-tools).

## Register a runtime

On **Agents**, create a runtime. Kinds:

| Value | In the form |
|---|---|
| `cursor_automation` | Cursor Automation (webhook) |
| `claude_ccr` | Claude CCR |
| `claude_ccma` | Claude CCMA, marked as later |
| `cursor_cloud` | Cursor Cloud, using the integration key rather than a pasted webhook secret |
| `grok_bot` | Grok Bots (webhook) |

Give it a name and an endpoint URL. Paste the webhook secret once. A later edit that leaves the secret blank keeps the stored secret. Disable a runtime from the same screen when it should stop receiving work. `GET /cockpit/api/runtimes?all=1` includes disabled rows.

**Instant task** on a runtime inserts a `todo` on that runtime's desk so the dispatcher wakes it.

## How work arrives

1. A task assigned to the runtime moves to `todo` (or a routine inserts one).
2. Dispatch calls the runtime's endpoint.
3. The agent clocks in with `work_clock_in`, then `task_claim` or `task_pickup`.
4. `task_pickup` returns the task, the project comments, and acknowledges unread handoff comments.
5. The agent heartbeats with `work_heartbeat`, logs with `work_log`, and finishes with `task_complete` or `task_request_close`, then `work_clock_out`.

`/work-items` shows the lease. **Queues** shows the tick, in-progress work, and queue depth. **Logs** shows tick history. **Routines** (`/settings/routines`) is where you enable a scheduled or instant job and bind it to a runtime. A disabled routine does not mint work.

## Close gate

`task_request_close` is the finish call.

- `human_approval_to_close` true: opens a close card. The task stays open until a person approves it.
- `human_approval_to_close` false: no card. The task can go to `done`. If a pull request is linked and your GitHub integration is connected, a pull request that is open with green checks can be merged as a merge commit as part of that close.

The default on create is false. Set it true when a person must accept the result. `task_request_promote` is the matching call to ask a person to move backlog work onto the board.

## Comments

Agents leave handoff notes with `comment_create` and drain them with `comment_list`, `comment_ack`, `comment_applied`, and `comment_dismiss`. People use the same comments on the task drawer. The comments inbox is `/comments`.

## Knowledge

The skill registry is [Knowledge](/docs/features/knowledge). Creating a skill from MCP (`skill_create`, `skills:write`) stores the markdown and queues a sync. That sync targets an external collection when the project is configured for it. Without that configuration the row still exists in chytr.

## Where work shows up

[Routines](/docs/features/routines) mint the scheduled jobs. [Queues](/docs/features/queues) show the tick. [Logs](/docs/features/logs) show tick history. [Work items](/docs/features/work-items) are the lease. Keys are issued on [API keys](/docs/features/api-keys).

## Agent bus

Runtimes that share a job can message each other with the `agent_bus_*` tools (scopes `agent_bus:read` and `agent_bus:write`). Subscribe, send or broadcast, read `agent_bus_inbox`, reply, and ack. This is separate from task comments.

## MCP tools

There is no MCP tool that registers a runtime. You create the runtime on this screen. The agent then calls:

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `work_clock_in` | `work:write` | Take the lease when dispatch fires |
| `task_claim` | `tasks:write` | Claim `todo` tasks for the runtime |
| `task_pickup` | `tasks:write`, `comments:read` | Claim plus handoff comments |
| `work_heartbeat` | `work:write` | Extend the lease |
| `task_request_close` | `tasks:write` | Finish, honoring the close gate |
| `work_clock_out` | `work:write` | Release the lease |

The bus tools are `agent_bus_subscribe`, `agent_bus_list_agents`, `agent_bus_broadcast`, `agent_bus_send`, `agent_bus_inbox`, `agent_bus_reply`, and `agent_bus_ack`.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/runtimes` | List or create. `?all=1` includes disabled |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/runtimes/:id` | Update. A blank secret keeps the stored one |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/runtimes/:id/disable` | Disable |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/runtimes/:id/instant-task` | Insert a `todo` so dispatch wakes the runtime |
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/runtimes/:id/sessions` | Sessions for the runtime |
| `POST` | `/api/mcp` | MCP JSON-RPC. Bearer token |
| `GET` | `/api/mcp` | OAuth metadata hint. Not a JSON-RPC call |
| `GET` | `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` | Public resource metadata |

Use your own host in place of `https://chytr.example.com`.

## Permissions

The webhook secret and the personal access token are different credentials. Token scopes come from one permission-set layer. The screen uses the signed-in session. MCP checks the bearer token.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `task_pickup` after dispatch, with the work item the runtime was given.

```json
{
  "tool": "task_pickup",
  "arguments": {
    "work_item_id": "lease-1",
    "claimed_by": "runtime-1"
  }
}
```

Expected result: the task, the project comments, and an acknowledgement of unread handoff comments. The call needs both `tasks:write` and `comments:read`. A runtime that was disabled on this screen does not receive new work.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "claimed_by": "runtime-1"
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/routines

# Routines

## What it does

Routines wake an agent on a schedule, so recurring work has a clock and a runtime without turning into a workflow template.

Open **Routines** (`/settings/routines`). A routine is a cron or instant job bound to a desk and a runtime. Enable it before it can mint work. A disabled routine does not. `/settings/jobs` redirects here.

This screen is not [Workflows](/docs/features/workflows). Templates instantiate tasks when they are applied. Routines are the other scheduler. `task_scheduled_create` attaches a cron to a task. It is not this registry.

The screen only calls the session API. There is no MCP tool that creates or enables a routine. An admin session does that here. Agents receive the tasks the routine mints.

## MCP tools

No MCP tool administers this registry. After a routine inserts a `todo`, the agent uses the task and work tools:

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `task_claim` | `tasks:write` | Claim the `todo` the routine minted |
| `task_pickup` | `tasks:write`, `comments:read` | Claim plus the handoff comments |
| `task_scheduled_create` | `schedules:write` | A different object: a cron on a task. Token only |
| `task_scheduled_enable` | `schedules:write` | Enable that scheduled task. Token only |

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/ops/jobs` | List or upsert. The screen calls this path |
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/ops/routines` | Same handlers as `/ops/jobs` |

`GET` returns both job planes and whether the master tick is on. Writes are admin-gated in the database. A non-admin session gets an admin-only error. The screen also reads `GET /cockpit/api/runtimes?all=1` when you bind a runtime.

## Permissions

Changing a routine requires an admin session. A personal access token cannot administer this screen. Task pickup still uses `tasks:write` from one permission-set layer. `schedules:write` is token-only and applies to scheduled tasks, not to this registry.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Do not look for a routine tool. Call `task_claim` for the runtime the routine dispatches.

```json
{
  "tool": "task_claim",
  "arguments": {
    "assignee_id": "runtime-1",
    "claimed_by": "runtime-1",
    "limit": 5
  }
}
```

Expected result: zero or more `todo` tasks assigned to that runtime, now claimed. An empty list means nothing is waiting. It does not mean the routine failed. Check the routine's enabled flag on this screen if work you expected never arrives.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "claimed": 1
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/knowledge

# Knowledge

## What it does

Knowledge is the skill registry, so an agent can load the procedure you wrote instead of guessing it from a chat.

Open **Knowledge** (`/settings/knowledge`). A skill is a markdown document with a slug, a family, and an enabled flag. You can dispatch one from the screen. Creating or updating from MCP stores the markdown and queues a sync. That sync targets an external collection only when the project is configured for it. Without that configuration the row still exists here.

The screen only calls the skill routes. The list and the body are the same records `skill_get` returns.

## MCP tools

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `skill_list` | `approvals:read` | List skills. Filters: `enabled_only`, `action_type`, `family`, `project_id` |
| `skill_get` | `approvals:read` | One skill by slug |
| `skill_metrics` | `approvals:read` | Recommendation agreement rates |
| `skill_create` | `skills:write` | Create a skill and queue a collection sync |
| `skill_update` | `skills:write` | Update a skill and queue a re-sync |

List and get use `approvals:read` on purpose. Create and update use `skills:write`. Holding only `skills:write` does not list the registry.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/skills` | List or create |
| `GET`, `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/skills/:id` | Read or update one skill |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/skills/:id/dispatch` | Dispatch the skill |
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/skill-families` | List or create a family |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/skill-families?id=` | Update a family |

## Permissions

Token scopes come from one permission-set layer, as the table shows. The screen uses the signed-in session.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `skill_get` with the slug before you follow the procedure.

```json
{
  "tool": "skill_get",
  "arguments": {
    "slug": "meeting-brief"
  }
}
```

Expected result: the skill's title, summary, and markdown body when that slug exists and is visible to the token. An unknown slug is an error, not an empty document. `skill_update` with `skill_id` queues a re-sync and does not require you to resend unchanged fields.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "slug": "meeting-brief",
  "title": "Meeting brief",
  "body_md": "Read the calendar row before you write the brief."
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/queues

# Queues

## What it does

Queues show whether work is waiting, running, or stuck, so you can repair the clock without reading a database.

Open **Queues** (`/queue`). The panel is the tick snapshot: queue depth, in-progress leases, and recent ticks. From here you can repair the heartbeat cron (`bootstrap`) or dispatch a tick now (`run_now`). You can also enable or disable a job on the cron plane. Binding a routine to a runtime is saved through the jobs route.

The screen only calls the session API. Agents do not administer the tick. They clock in when a task arrives. See [Work items](/docs/features/work-items) and [Routines](/docs/features/routines).

## MCP tools

No MCP tool reads or repairs this queue. The agent-facing lease tools are `work_status` (`work:read`) and `work_heartbeat` (`work:write`). They describe one lease, not the operator snapshot on this screen.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/queue` | Snapshot the screen renders |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/queue/heartbeat` | Body `action` is `bootstrap` or `run_now` |
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/ops/jobs` | Jobs shown beside the queue |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/ops/jobs` | Enable or disable a job, or set a binding |

`POST /cockpit/api/queue/bind` exists for setting or clearing a job's primary runtime. This screen writes bindings through `/cockpit/api/ops/jobs`.

## Permissions

The screen uses the signed-in session. Job writes are admin-gated in the database, same as [Routines](/docs/features/routines). A token's permission sets do not grant this screen. Lease tools still use `work:read` and `work:write`.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

There is no queue tool. Call `work_status` for the lease you hold.

```json
{
  "tool": "work_status",
  "arguments": {
    "kind": "task",
    "ref": "desk-1:send-scope"
  }
}
```

Expected result: that lease's status and last heartbeat, or an empty result when nothing is claimed for that kind and ref. Send only one selector. Adding `run_id` in the same call is rejected.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "kind": "task",
  "ref": "desk-1:send-scope",
  "status": "claimed"
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/logs

# Logs

## What it does

Logs show whether the clock fired and how the last runs finished, so a quiet agent is either idle or stuck and you can tell which.

Open **Logs** (`/logs`). Two reads share the page. One is heartbeat ticks and recent work-item runs. The other is hook stats over the last 168 hours: which tools were called, how many failed, and when the last call was. Filter ticks by kind (`tick`, `manual`, `bootstrap`, `dispatch`) and runs by status (`running`, `claimed`, `pending`, `done`, `failed`, `timed_out`, `skipped`).

The screen is read-only. Agents append lines on their own lease with `work_log`. That is the write path. This page is the read path.

## MCP tools

No MCP tool returns this page's tick history. The write an agent does have:

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `work_log` | `work:write` | Append a line on a lease and bump the heartbeat |
| `work_status` | `work:read` | Read that lease |

Hook stats are session-only.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/logs` | Ticks and recent runs |
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/agent-hook-stats?hours=168` | Tool-call stats. The screen asks for 168 hours |

Both are GET. A failed hook-stats call does not blank the tick list.

## Permissions

The screen uses the signed-in session. `work_log` needs `work:write` from one permission-set layer. There is no logs scope.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `work_log` on the lease you clocked in, not on the logs route.

```json
{
  "tool": "work_log",
  "arguments": {
    "work_item_id": "lease-1",
    "level": "info",
    "message": "Draft stored. Waiting on the approval."
  }
}
```

Expected result: the line is appended and the lease heartbeat moves forward. The Logs screen shows that run on refresh. A log call for a lease the token does not hold is rejected.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "level": "info"
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/llms

# LLMs

## What it does

LLMs is the registry of named model instances and the providers they call. Each instance pins a model id on a provider for one flow and one role (`primary`, `shadow`, or `escalation`). A swap is an edit of that row. You do not deploy code to change the model.

Open **LLMs** (`/settings/llms`). The screen has two parts:

- **Providers** — a key, an `https` endpoint, an enabled flag, and an optional API token. The token is written to Vault. The screen never shows it again. `has_vault` is true when a token is stored.
- **Named instances** — instance name, flow, role, provider, pinned model id, a JSON params object, and an enabled flag.

This app does not call the provider. Edge workers resolve the instance and pull the key. Uncheck **Enabled**, or use Disable, to stop that path. The stored token stays.

A blank token on edit keeps the stored secret. A new provider can be saved with no token; edge hops then have no key until you paste one.

One instance per flow and role. To point the same flow at a different pinned model, edit the existing row. Floating aliases such as `latest` are rejected.

Provider API tokens are not agent personal access tokens. Issue agent tokens under **API Keys**. Register webhook runtimes under **Agents**.

## MCP tools

List tools need `decisions:read`. Create, update, and disable need `decisions:write`. The database still requires the token's user to be a workspace owner or admin, so the scope alone cannot rotate a key.

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `llm_provider_list` | `decisions:read` | Providers. `has_vault` only |
| `llm_provider_create` | `decisions:write` | Create. Optional token goes to Vault |
| `llm_provider_update` | `decisions:write` | Update. Blank token keeps the secret |
| `llm_provider_disable` | `decisions:write` | Kill switch. Secret stays |
| `llm_binding_list` | `decisions:read` | Instances plus flow options |
| `llm_binding_create` | `decisions:write` | Create a pinned instance |
| `llm_binding_update` | `decisions:write` | Update by id. Omitted fields stay |
| `llm_binding_disable` | `decisions:write` | Kill switch. Row stays |

Re-enable with `llm_provider_update` or `llm_binding_update` and `enabled: true`.

## HTTP endpoints

Session routes. Same rules as the screen: no Vault id, no raw token, in the response.

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/llms/providers` | List providers |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/llms/providers` | Create. Optional `token` |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/llms/providers/:providerKey` | Update. Blank `token` keeps the secret |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/llms/providers/:providerKey/disable` | Disable |
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/llms/bindings` | Instances and flows |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/llms/bindings` | Create. `modelId` must be pinned |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/llms/bindings/:id` | Update |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/llms/bindings/:id/disable` | Disable |

A provider response looks like `{ "ok": true, "provider": { "provider_key": "example-provider", "endpoint_url": "https://api.example.com/v1", "enabled": false, "has_vault": true } }`.

## Permissions

The signed-in user must be a workspace owner or admin. Members get a refusal from the registry calls.

MCP uses the existing decision scopes, not a separate key system:

- `decisions:read` — list providers and instances
- `decisions:write` — create, update, disable

The token user must also be an owner or admin. An agent personal access token is not a provider API token. Do not paste an agent token into the provider token field.

There is no route that returns the stored provider secret to the browser or to MCP.

## Agent example

Create a provider with a placeholder token, then a pinned instance. `enabled` stays false until you mean to use it.

```json
{
  "name": "llm_provider_create",
  "arguments": {
    "provider_key": "example-provider",
    "endpoint_url": "https://api.example.com/v1",
    "enabled": false,
    "token": "paste-provider-token"
  }
}
```

Expected result: the provider row, `has_vault` true, and no token field.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "provider": {
    "provider_key": "example-provider",
    "endpoint_url": "https://api.example.com/v1",
    "enabled": false,
    "has_vault": true
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "name": "llm_binding_create",
  "arguments": {
    "instance_name": "example-classify",
    "flow_key": "activity.quality",
    "role": "primary",
    "provider_key": "example-provider",
    "model_id": "claude-sonnet-5",
    "params": {},
    "enabled": false
  }
}
```

Expected result: one binding. A second `primary` on the same flow is refused. Edit the first row to change the pinned model id. `llm_binding_disable` with `{ "id": "binding-id" }` turns that row off and leaves it in the list.

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/classifiers

# Classifiers

## What it does

Classifiers are named flows with a pinned question set. Each question has a closed answer space: choice, score, or yes/no. A decision returns those typed answers plus a confidence and a gate. It does not parse free text at the act layer.

Open **Classifiers** (`/settings/classifiers`). You can create a flow, edit its description and enabled flag, save a new question-set version, and pin a version. Question sets are content-hashed. Saving an edit writes the next version instead of rewriting the old one. Usage (runs, gate mix, confidence, cost) stays on the same page and does not change a flow.

**Archive a flow.** Each flow has an **Archive** button in its row and in its open drawer. A confirmation names the flow first. Archiving forces the flow disabled, so it stops running, and hides it from the list. Runs, answers, and question-set versions stay. Tick **Show archived** to see archived flows, then **Restore** one. A restored flow comes back disabled; enable it yourself. An archived flow cannot be edited until it is restored. Only the flow's owner or an admin can archive or restore. Anyone else gets a permission error. A flow with no owner (seeded) is admin only.

Thresholds and per-gate actions stay on [Decision flows](/docs/features/decision-flows). The audit of what already ran is [Decisions](/docs/features/decisions).

The screen only calls the classifier routes. Agents use the same RPCs through the tools below.

## MCP tools

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `classifier_flows_list` | `classifiers:read` | List flows and question-set versions. `can_edit` is true when the caller may write |
| `classifier_flow_get` | `classifiers:read` | Read one flow by `flow_key` |
| `classifier_flow_create` | `classifiers:write` | Create a flow and its first pinned question set. New flows start disabled |
| `classifier_flow_update` | `classifiers:write` | Edit description, enabled, act policy, or the act allow list. An archived flow returns an error until restored |
| `classifier_flow_archive` | `classifiers:write` | Archive (soft delete) a flow, or restore it with `archived: false`. Owner or admin only |
| `classifier_question_set_create` | `classifiers:write` | Append a version. `pin: true` points the flow at it. The same content returns the existing version |
| `classifier_question_set_pin` | `classifiers:write` | Pin a version that already belongs to the flow |

`bool` in a question is stored as `noul`. `choice` needs 2 to 24 choices. `score` defaults to 0..1.

Agent PATs carry these scopes on the token. A signed-in app session uses the user's permission set instead. An admin set in the app can edit without a separate classifiers scope. That bypass does not apply to a PAT.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/classifiers/stats` | Per-flow usage. Any signed-in session. Does not change a flow |
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/classifiers/flows` | List (`?include_archived=true` adds archived flows), or create `{ flow_key, description, questions }` |
| `GET`, `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/classifiers/flows/:flowKey` | Read, or edit metadata |
| `POST`, `DELETE` | `/cockpit/api/classifiers/flows/:flowKey/archive` | Archive, or restore. Owner or admin only |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/classifiers/flows/:flowKey/question-sets` | Append a version. Body `{ questions, pin? }` |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/classifiers/flows/:flowKey/question-sets/:id/pin` | Pin that version |

`POST` create returns 201. A missing permission returns 403. An unknown flow returns 404. A duplicate `flow_key` returns 409. Editing an archived flow returns 409. A question that is not choice, score, or bool returns 400.

The stats response is `{ "ok": true, "flows": [ ... ] }`. Each flow includes gate counts (`auto`, `hold`, `escalate`, `blocked_by_rule`), confidence buckets, and cost or token fields when they were stored. An empty list means no scored runs yet, not a broken page.

## Permissions

List and read need `classifiers:read` (or `classifiers:write`). Create, update, and pin need `classifiers:write`. On a chytr session, an admin permission set in the app may do both. Grant the scopes on a permission set for anyone else. PAT callers need the scope on the token. Usage stats use the signed-in session and do not check these scopes.

Row access for recorded decisions stays RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `classifier_flow_create` with a closed question set.

```json
{
  "tool": "classifier_flow_create",
  "arguments": {
    "flow_key": "demo.route",
    "description": "Route a note to a desk.",
    "enabled": false,
    "questions": {
      "desk": {
        "type": "choice",
        "choices": ["sales", "delivery"]
      },
      "is_customer": {
        "type": "bool"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Expected result: a disabled flow, one question-set version, and `is_customer` stored as `noul`. `classifier_question_set_create` with `pin` true adds the next version and points the flow at it. The same questions again do not add a version.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "can_edit": true,
  "flow": {
    "flow_key": "demo.route",
    "enabled": false
  }
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/decision-flows

# Decision flows

## What it does

Decision flows declare how a classification becomes an action, so a gate can hold, escalate, or do nothing without hiding that choice in code.

Open **Decision Flows** (`/settings/decision-flows`). The list loads every flow from `GET /cockpit/api/decisions/graph`. **+ New flow** (admins) creates a disabled flow with one yes/no question and thresholds at 1.0. The act allowlist starts empty: mint, enqueue, and patch stay unchecked until an admin opts in on the saved flow. **Configure** opens the editor at `/decisions/<flowKey>`.

The editor loads the flow, model bindings, thresholds, and the action on each gate (`auto`, `hold`, `escalate`, `blocked_by_rule`). Fields stay read-only unless `can_edit` is true, and nothing is saved until you press Save.

The path canvas is one vertical column: trigger, then decide, then gate, then act, with an arrow between each step. A recorded run highlights that path as one line. **Test** dry-runs the saved thresholds against a confidence fixture and highlights the path it took. Test does not call a provider, write a run, or fire the act.

This object is not a [Workflow](/docs/features/workflows) template. The audit of what already ran is [Decisions](/docs/features/decisions).

## MCP tools

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `decision_flow_list` | `decisions:read` | Every flow, plus `can_create` |
| `decision_flow_get` | `decisions:read` | One flow and its `live_path` |
| `decision_flow_create` | `decisions:write` | Admin create. Lands disabled. Does not run it |
| `decision_flow_test` | `decisions:read` | Dry-run fixture answers. Returns the path highlight |

`decision_flow_test` and the HTTP test route share one eval. Both set `dry_run: true` and `executed: false`.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/decisions/graph` | List flows. Includes `can_create` |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/decisions/graph` | Create `{ flow_key, description }`. Optional `questions` |
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/decisions/graph/:flowKey` | Load the editor. Includes `can_edit` and `live_path` |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/decisions/graph/:flowKey` | Save enabled flag, act policy, allow list, and binding toggles |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/decisions/graph/:flowKey/test` | Dry-run `{ answers: [{ question_key, confidence }] }` |

`GET` on an unknown key returns 404. `PATCH` and create return 403 when the session cannot edit or create. A duplicate `flow_key` returns 409.

## Permissions

The screen uses the signed-in session. Any signed-in user can list and open a flow. `can_edit` is admin or the flow owner. `can_create` is admin. MCP uses the existing `decisions:read` and `decisions:write` scopes. Test is a read: it writes nothing.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

List, then dry-run the seeded flow at the boundary confidence.

```json
{
  "tool": "decision_flow_list"
}
```

```json
{
  "tool": "decision_flow_test",
  "arguments": {
    "flow_key": "activity.quality",
    "answers": [{ "question_key": "quality_class", "confidence": 1 }]
  }
}
```

Expected result: `verdict` is `auto` when confidence is at least the saved threshold, otherwise `hold`. `path` is `trigger`, `decide`, `gate:<verdict>`, `act:<type>`. `executed` is false. Nodes with `live: true` are the highlighted path.

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/decisions

# Decisions

## What it does

Decisions show how activity quality was classified, so a shadow result can disagree with the live label without silently changing it.

Open **Decisions** (`/decisions`). Each row is one classification: when it ran, the activity, shadow versus live quality, confidence, and the gate (`auto`, `hold`, `escalate`, or `blocked_by_rule`). Filter by gate, or by whether the shadow agrees with the live label. The row links to the decision record and, when one exists, the approval.

This page does not approve extraction cards. That queue is [Approvals](/docs/features/approvals). Configuring the flow is [Decision flows](/docs/features/decision-flows). How extraction files cards is [Meetings and extraction](/docs/features/meetings).

The screen only reads one session route. There is no MCP tool for this audit.

## MCP tools

No MCP tool lists these rows. Agents that review extraction proposals use `extraction_pending` and `extraction_review` (`approvals:read` and `approvals:write`). Those tools resolve cards. They do not rewrite this audit.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/decisions/rank1?limit=200` | Rows for this screen |

The screen loads up to 200 rows and filters gate and agreement in the browser. The route is GET only.

## Permissions

The screen uses the signed-in session. There is no decisions-audit scope on the permission-set layer. Extraction review, if you use it, needs `approvals:write`.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

There is no tool call for this table. A session client reads the same route.

```json
{
  "method": "GET",
  "path": "/cockpit/api/decisions/rank1?limit=200"
}
```

Expected result: `{ "ok": true, "rows": [ ... ] }`. A row's gate is one of `auto`, `hold`, `escalate`, or `blocked_by_rule`. An empty `rows` array means nothing has been classified into this audit. It does not mean extraction is off.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "rows": [
    {
      "gate_verdict": "hold",
      "shadow_disagreement": true,
      "live_quality_class": "substantive",
      "quality_class": "transactional"
    }
  ]
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/workflows

# Workflows

## What it does

Workflows turn a named recipe into tasks on a desk, so a repeated motion starts the same way every time.

A workflow template is a named recipe: a desk, a description, steps, and an optional trigger. Applying it creates a parent task and child tasks on that desk. It does not run arbitrary code inside the template step. The shipped step type creates tasks.

Open **Automations → Workflows** (`/settings/workflows`). You can list templates, filter by status, and edit one in the drawer. The API is under `/cockpit/api/workflows`.

This screen is not **Decision flows**. Decision flows are a different object, on `/settings/decision-flows`.

## Applying a template

`workflow_apply` (scope `workflows:write`) instantiates a template into tasks. In the product this is how a person or an agent starts the recipe against a project. Pass the template id and the context project (the desk the tasks should land on).

`workflow_template_create` upserts the template and its steps.

## Triggers

A template can carry a declarative trigger: a predicate, a JSON `input_schema`, and a `trigger_mode`.

| Mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `shadow_match` | Default. The predicate is evaluated and a `would_start` event is recorded. No tasks are created. `workflow_trigger_enable` applies this mode immediately |
| `live` | The trigger may start the template, but only after a go-live approval. `workflow_trigger_enable` with `mode` `live` mints a pending card of type `workflow_trigger_go_live` and leaves `trigger_mode` unchanged until that card is approved. A second live request while the card is pending returns the same card. `activities` triggers and `engine=pgflow` refuse live and mint nothing |

So a saved trigger does not start work until that template is live and the go-live card is approved. Inspect events with `GET /cockpit/api/workflows/<id>/trigger/events`. Dry-run with `POST …/trigger/dry-run`. Enqueue a manual run with `POST …/trigger`, or with MCP `workflow_trigger`.

`workflow_trigger_describe` returns the input contract for a template. Workspace for the trigger tools comes from the personal access token binding. Do not pass `workspace_id`. The caller needs a token bound to the template's workspace.

Older activity-matching filters (`metadata.filter`) still exist on the classic enqueue path. New triggers should use the declarative trigger and input schema. Both can be present during this phase.

`flow_start` and `flow_run_status` are the lower-level pgflow run controls (scope `workflows:write`). Use the template tools unless you are operating a registered flow slug directly.

## Scheduled tasks

`task_scheduled_create` and `task_scheduled_enable` (scope `schedules:write`, personal access token only) attach a cron schedule to a task, optionally pointing it at a workflow template. Enable it before the schedule fires. Routines under **Agents → Routines** are the other scheduler: a cron or instant job bound to a runtime. They are not workflow templates.

## What is not in the product yet

Schedule-shaped and webhook-shaped triggers beyond the activity predicate, and a full retirement of the older per-flow doors, are not the behavior the app ships. If the drawer does not show a control, it is not a supported way to start work. Named models are [LLMs](/docs/features/llms). That registry does not configure these templates. Routines are [Routines](/docs/features/routines). Classifiers are [Classifiers](/docs/features/classifiers).

## MCP tools

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `workflow_template_create` | `workflows:write` | Create or update a template and its steps. Token only |
| `workflow_apply` | `workflows:write` | Instantiate tasks on a desk. Token only |
| `workflow_trigger_describe` | `workflows:read` | Input contract. Workspace comes from the token binding |
| `workflow_trigger` | `workflows:write` | Enqueue a trigger with validated input. Workspace comes from the token binding |
| `workflow_trigger_objects` | `workflows:read` | Tables a trigger can watch. Workspace comes from the token binding |
| `workflow_trigger_list` | `workflows:read` | Triggers in the token's workspace |
| `workflow_trigger_events` | `workflows:read` | Recent trigger events |
| `workflow_trigger_test` | `workflows:read` | Dry-run against an existing row. Writes nothing |
| `workflow_trigger_save` | `workflows:write` | Create or update a trigger. Saved disabled. Token only |
| `workflow_trigger_enable` | `workflows:write` | Enable, or set `shadow_match` now. `live` mints `workflow_trigger_go_live` and does not flip the mode. Token only |
| `flow_start` | `workflows:write` | Start a registered flow by slug |
| `flow_run_status` | `workflows:write` | Poll a run and its steps |

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/workflows` | List or create templates |
| `GET`, `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/workflows/:id` | Read or edit |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/workflows/:id/trigger` | Enqueue a trigger |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/workflows/:id/trigger/dry-run` | Validate without starting |
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/workflows/:id/trigger/events` | Trigger event log |

The screen only calls these routes. Applying a template from an agent uses `workflow_apply`.

## Permissions

Token scopes come from one permission-set layer. Reads need `workflows:read`. Writes need `workflows:write` and are token-only. The screen uses the signed-in session.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `workflow_trigger_describe` before you enqueue.

```json
{
  "tool": "workflow_trigger_describe",
  "arguments": {
    "template": "calendar-brief"
  }
}
```

Expected result: the input contract for that template. `workflow_trigger` with a body that fails the contract does not start tasks. A template still in `shadow_match` records a `would_start` event and does not create tasks. `workflow_trigger_enable` with `mode` `live` returns a pending `workflow_trigger_go_live` card and leaves the mode unchanged.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "template": "calendar-brief",
  "trigger_mode": "shadow_match"
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/integrations

# Integrations

## What it does

Integrations connect the providers chytr already knows how to sync, so mail, calendar, pull requests, and posts show up without pasting a secret into a prompt.

Open **Integrations** (`/settings/integrations`). You can connect or disconnect Google, GitHub, and X, and store the Cursor Cloud settings the runtime uses. Disconnect revokes the stored connection. Connecting a provider does not create users and does not grant MCP scopes.

Secrets stay on the server. The screen never returns a refresh token to the browser after connect. The page only calls the session routes below. There is no MCP tool that connects a provider. What chytr does with a connected GitHub, such as merging a task's pull requests when it closes, is on [GitHub](/docs/features/github).

## MCP tools

No MCP tool connects or revokes an integration. Agents call chytr with a personal access token from [API keys](/docs/features/api-keys). That token is not a Google, GitHub, or X credential. Provider access stays on this screen.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/integrations` | Connection status for the workspace |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/connect` | Start a provider connect |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/revoke` | Disconnect a provider |
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/cursor` | Read or save Cursor Cloud settings |
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/chytr` | Log-drain settings |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/chytr/test` | Test the drain |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/integrations/chytr/backfill` | Backfill the drain |

## Permissions

The screen uses the signed-in session for the workspace. A personal access token cannot connect a provider. Permission sets do not include a provider-admin scope. After a provider is connected, data it syncs still follows RLS: admins see all rows, members see their own.

## Agent example

There is no tool call. A session client reads status.

```json
{
  "method": "GET",
  "path": "/cockpit/api/integrations"
}
```

Expected result: active connections, without stored secrets. Each item names a `provider` (`google`, `github`, or `x`). `revoke` removes that connection. Later syncs stop. Rows already imported stay until you delete them.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "connections": [
    { "provider": "google", "label": "Workspace" }
  ]
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/api-keys

# API keys

## What it does

API keys let an agent call MCP as you, with only the scopes you put on the key, so a leaked token can be revoked without changing your password.

Open **API Keys** (`/settings/keys`). A key is a personal access token. The value starts with `cbpat_` and is shown once. Store it outside the repo and outside the chat. Effective scopes are the union of the permission sets you attach plus any extra scopes. That union is what MCP checks. You can replace the sets or the extras later. Revoke is immediate for new calls.

TTL choices are 1 hour, 24 hours, 7 days (the form default), 30 days, or forever. OAuth sessions do not use this string. They use the signed-in user's scopes. Some writes, including `files:write`, `schedules:write`, and `workflows:write`, are token-only.

The screen only calls the session API. Nothing in MCP issues a key. You create the key here, then the agent sends it as `Authorization: Bearer`.

How scopes map to tools is in [Permissions and API keys](/docs/reference/permissions). Connecting the runtime that receives work is in [Connecting agents](/docs/features/agents).

## MCP tools

No MCP tool creates, lists, or revokes tokens. A token is the credential that calls every other tool. Issuing one from inside a tool would hide the one-time secret in a log.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/tokens` | List your keys, or issue one. Plaintext is only in the create response |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/tokens/:id/revoke` | Revoke |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/tokens/:id/scopes` | Replace extra scopes |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/tokens/:id/sets` | Replace permission-set membership |

`GET` also returns the scope catalog and the active permission sets so the form can render checkboxes.

## Permissions

Any signed-in member can issue and revoke their own keys. The sets they attach are the one permission-set layer. There is no second role matrix inside the token. A revoked key fails the next MCP call. A key that was already exchanged for a short-lived access token stays valid until that access token expires.

Row access on the data the key reads is still RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own. The key does not widen RLS. Workflow trigger tools take the workspace from this token's binding. Do not pass `workspace_id`.

## Agent example

Create the key in the screen, then call MCP with it. This example lists approvals. It does not create a key.

```json
{
  "tool": "approval_list",
  "arguments": {
    "status": "pending",
    "limit": 5
  }
}
```

Expected result with `approvals:read` on the key: pending cards for that owner, up to five. The token string is not echoed back. A revoked key returns an auth error and an empty list is not the same thing. An empty list with `ok` true means there is nothing pending.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "approvals": []
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/users

# Users and members

## What it does

Users are the people who can sign in, so an owner can invite a teammate and a member cannot administer the workspace.

**Admin → Users** (`/settings/users`) lists the people in the current workspace. An owner or an admin can invite, change a role, and deactivate. A member cannot administer this screen. Calls go through workspace membership checks. A personal access token cannot administer users.

## Roles

| Role | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `owner` | The installing membership. The last owner cannot be removed or demoted by the membership trigger |
| `admin` | Can invite, change roles, and deactivate, same as an owner, on this screen |
| `member` | Can use chytr. Cannot administer members |

Invite by email. If the person already has an Auth user, they are added. If they do not, chytr sends an Auth invite and then adds the membership. The invite link returns them to `/login` on your app origin. They still sign in with a one-time code. The login form does not sign up a stranger who was never invited.

Deactivate revokes that person's personal access tokens, removes their permission-set grants, and disables the membership. An access token that was already issued stays valid until it expires.

`user_profiles.is_admin` is a database flag, separate from the workspace `admin` role. `extraction_threshold_set` checks it: `is_admin()` for a session, `is_admin_for` for a token. On a running workspace, the Users role is the membership control. Threshold and token behavior is in [Permissions and API keys](/docs/reference/permissions).

## What a member can see

Role decides what you can administer. Row-level security decides which records you see.

- **Admins and owners** see every row in the workspace.
- **Members** see the rows they created.
- A member can use the feature screens, but cannot administer people: the Users screen and Permission sets need an owner or admin.
- A personal access token sees what its scopes allow, and no more than the person who issued it.

If a record you expect is missing, the likely cause is that it belongs to someone else. Ask an admin.

## Domains

Labels live on [Domains](/docs/features/domains). They filter tasks and projects. They do not grant permissions.

## Permission sets on a person

[Permission sets](/docs/features/permission-sets) can attach sets to a user. One permission layer covers the app and a signed-in user's API token. The person's permission set is that layer. Agent MCP tokens stay separate and keep the sets and extras on the token.

**Status.** That attachment is behind `app_settings` key `feature.permission_sets_users`, and the flag defaults off. While it is off, the user-grant table is not the enforcement path. A user JWT on MCP holds the read floor. Tokens carry their own scopes. Details are in [Permissions and API keys](/docs/reference/permissions).

## Rows a member can see

A row belongs to the person who created it. Members see their own rows. Admins and owners see every row. Sharing comes later. The column is `owner_user_id`, stamped on insert.

**Status.** That creator rule is the model. Approvals already use it, plus `is_admin()` and a token scope. Core CRM policies are still wider than "rows I created." See [Row access](/docs/reference/permissions#row-access).

## Integrations

Provider connections are [Integrations](/docs/features/integrations). Connecting a provider does not create users.

## Notifications

The in-app inbox is [Notifications](/docs/features/notifications).

## MCP tools

No MCP tool invites, demotes, or deactivates a member. A personal access token cannot administer this screen. Every verb goes through workspace membership checks on the session.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/users` | List members, or invite, change a role, or deactivate |

`POST` is limited to an active workspace owner or admin. A member's call is rejected.

## Permissions

This screen is workspace role, not a token scope. Owner and admin can invite, change roles, and deactivate. A member cannot. Deactivate revokes that person's personal access tokens and permission-set grants.

Row access elsewhere is the creator model in [Permissions and API keys](/docs/reference/permissions#row-access). Approvals already follow it. Other CRM tables are still wider. Membership here is what makes someone an admin or a member. The workspace role is not `is_admin()`.

## Agent example

There is no tool call. A session client lists members.

```json
{
  "method": "GET",
  "path": "/cockpit/api/users"
}
```

Expected result for an owner or admin: the workspace members and their roles (`owner`, `admin`, `member`). A member's session is rejected. The payload does not include a token secret.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "members": [
    { "role": "owner" },
    { "role": "member" }
  ]
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/permission-sets

# Permission sets

## What it does

Permission sets bundle scopes so a token carries one list of what it may call, and you do not keep a second permission system beside it.

Open **Perm Sets** (`/settings/permission-sets`). A set has a slug, a name, and a list of scopes from `pat_scopes`. Seeded slugs include `mcp-readonly`, `cockpit-ops`, and `crm-read`. You can change them after install. A retired scope stays in the catalog so old tokens can be understood, and it is not offered for new grants.

Creating, editing, and archiving a set requires an admin session. The built-in `admin` set cannot be renamed or archived. Attaching a set directly to a user, instead of to a token, is behind `app_settings` key `feature.permission_sets_users`. That flag defaults off. While it is off, the user-grant table is not the enforcement path. Tokens are.

The screen only calls the session API. MCP checks the scopes on the token at call time. It does not read a second role table.

The catalog and the human-only approval rule are in [Permissions and API keys](/docs/reference/permissions). Issuing a key is [API keys](/docs/features/api-keys).

## MCP tools

No MCP tool edits permission sets. A token cannot widen itself. Admin changes happen on this screen.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/permission-sets` | List sets and the scope catalog. `?archived=1` includes archived sets |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/permission-sets` | Create a set |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/permission-sets` | Update or archive a set |
| `GET`, `POST` | `/cockpit/api/permission-sets/admin` | User-grant operations when that flag is on |

Writes return 403 when the session is not an admin. Renaming or archiving the built-in `admin` set is refused even for an admin.

## Permissions

This screen is the permission-set layer. Scopes on a token are the union of its sets plus extra scopes. There is no parallel profile or graph role for MCP. User grants stay off unless you turn the flag on.

Data the token then reads is still RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own. A broad scope does not override that.

## Agent example

There is no tool call that edits a set. After an admin puts `approvals:read` on the set attached to your key, call `approval_list`.

```json
{
  "tool": "approval_list",
  "arguments": {
    "status": "pending",
    "limit": 1
  }
}
```

Expected result: the call succeeds when the set includes `approvals:read`. The same call without that scope is rejected. Changing the set does not change rows you are not allowed to see under RLS.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "approvals": []
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/domains

# Domains

## What it does

Domains are labels you define, so tasks, projects, and comments can be filtered by the same short code.

Open **Domains** (`/settings/domains`). A domain has a code, a label, a color, and a sort order. The code does not change after create. You can archive a code and restore it. Archiving hides it from pickers. It does not delete the tasks that used it.

A domain is not a permission and not an email domain. It does not grant scopes. The [Dash](/docs/features/dash) domain filter uses this catalog.

The screen only calls the session API. There is no MCP tool that creates labels. Agents pass a domain code that already exists, for example on `task_create`.

## MCP tools

No MCP tool administers this catalog. Tools that accept a domain code:

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `task_create` | `tasks:write` | Optional `domain` on a new task |
| `task_list` | `tasks:read` | Filter `domain` |
| `comment_create` | `comments:write` | Optional `domain` on a comment |

An unknown code is not created on the fly.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/domains` | List the catalog |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/domains` | Create. Body includes `code`, `label`, `color`, `sort_order` |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/domains/:code` | Update label, color, sort, or `archived` |

Color is `#rrggbb`. Writes require an owner or admin session. A member gets 403.

## Permissions

Catalog writes are an owner or admin session, not a token scope. There is no domains scope on the permission-set layer. Tasks and comments still need their own scopes.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own. The catalog itself is workspace-wide for people who can open the screen.

## Agent example

Call `task_list` with a code you read from this screen. Do not invent one.

```json
{
  "tool": "task_list",
  "arguments": {
    "domain": "delivery",
    "status": "todo",
    "limit": 20
  }
}
```

Expected result: todo tasks tagged `delivery` that this token may see. An empty list means nothing is in that label, not that the label is missing. Creating the label is the POST above, from an admin session.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "tasks": []
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/approval-types

# Approval types

## What it does

Approval types define the shape of a create or update card, so an agent can send only the fields you allow and the rest are dropped.

Open **Approval types** (`/settings/approvals`). You edit entity shapes and the contract for each card type. The queue that uses those shapes is [Approvals](/docs/features/approvals). The field lists are also in [Entity fields](/docs/reference/entity-fields).

Duplicate protection on create skips the insert when the slug or domain is already present. Keys that are not in the shape are dropped. This screen is where you change the shape. It does not resolve cards.

The page only calls one pair of session routes. There is no MCP tool that edits shapes. An agent that needs a new field asks a person to add it here, then sends that field on the next card.

## MCP tools

No MCP tool edits shapes. Agents file cards with `approval_create` (`approvals:write`) and must stay inside the shape this screen stores. `approval_list` (`approvals:read`) shows the pending cards. It does not show the shape editor.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/approval-shapes` | Shapes and type contracts |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/approval-shapes` | Save an edit |

Both use the signed-in session. The queue itself is `/cockpit/api/approvals`, documented on [Approvals](/docs/features/approvals).

## Permissions

Editing shapes uses the signed-in session. Filing a card needs `approvals:write` from one permission-set layer. Changing a shape does not grant an agent permission to approve a human-only type.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `approval_create` with fields the shape allows. Leave out keys the shape does not list.

```json
{
  "tool": "approval_create",
  "arguments": {
    "item_type": "graph_entity_create",
    "title": "Create contact: Jane Example",
    "table": "contacts",
    "fields": {
      "full_name": "Jane Example",
      "title": "VP Operations",
      "lifecycle_stage": "lead"
    }
  }
}
```

Expected result: a pending card. Fields not in the contact shape are dropped, not stored on the side. The contact row appears only after a person approves the card.

```json
{
  "status": "pending",
  "item_type": "graph_entity_create"
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/kg-health

# KG Health

## What it does

KG Health shows whether the graph is intact, so you can see missing links and extraction gaps before they turn into bad proposals.

Open **KG Health** (`/health`). Tiles cover entity counts, hygiene, recent decisions, and extraction gaps. A gap is something the pipeline noticed and did not finish. This page does not resolve it. Resolution is an approval card. See [Approvals](/docs/features/approvals) and [Meetings and extraction](/docs/features/meetings).

The meeting ingest lane has its own panel on [Meeting pipeline](/docs/features/meeting-pipeline). Do not treat these counts as that lane's health.

The screen only reads one session route. It does not write.

## MCP tools

No MCP tool returns this page. `cockpit_get` (`cockpit:read`) includes knowledge-graph health counts inside the home aggregate. That is the agent-readable summary. It is not the full gap list on this screen. Extraction volume is `extraction_metrics` (`approvals:read`).

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/health` | `{ "ok": true, "kb_health": { ... } }` |

`kb_health` includes `entity_counts` or `hygiene.entity_counts`, `extraction_gaps` (`count` and `items`), and `decisions` (including `last_5`). Empty gaps mean nothing is waiting, not that the route failed.

## Permissions

The screen uses the signed-in session. `cockpit_get` needs `cockpit:read`. `extraction_metrics` needs `approvals:read`. Both come from one permission-set layer.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own. Counts follow that scope.

## Agent example

Call `cockpit_get` when you need the summary an agent is allowed to see.

```json
{
  "tool": "cockpit_get",
  "arguments": {}
}
```

Expected result: an aggregate that includes health counts for the token's owner. It will not include another member's gaps. For the full gap list, a person opens `/health`. The tool does not clear a gap.

```json
{
  "kb_health": {
    "extraction_gaps": {
      "count": 0
    }
  }
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/meeting-pipeline

# Meeting pipeline

## What it does

Meeting pipeline shows whether meetings are making it into chytr, so a gap in the lane is visible before you look for a missing note.

Open **Meeting Pipeline** (`/meeting-pipeline`). The panel is lane health: what synced, what is still drifting, and where extraction stands. Sync drift means meetings the calendar knows about that are not in the database yet. This page is not the review queue. Proposals wait on [Approvals](/docs/features/approvals). The extraction contract is [Meetings and extraction](/docs/features/meetings). Graph-wide counts are [KG Health](/docs/features/kg-health).

The screen only reads one session route. It does not ingest a meeting and it does not approve a card.

## MCP tools

No MCP tool returns this panel. Agents submit a meeting with `meeting_graph_checkin` (`graph:write`) and read extraction volume with `extraction_metrics` (`approvals:read`). Those calls do not replace the drift counts on this screen.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/pipeline-health` | `{ "ok": true, "pipeline_health": { ... } }` |

The route is GET only. Drift is reported as meetings not yet in the database. It is not a list you edit here.

## Permissions

The screen uses the signed-in session. Check-in needs `graph:write`. Extraction metrics need `approvals:read`. Both come from one permission-set layer.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows. Members see their own.

## Agent example

Call `extraction_metrics` for the review backlog. Open this screen when you need drift.

```json
{
  "tool": "extraction_metrics",
  "arguments": {
    "days": 7
  }
}
```

Expected result: counts by extraction action type for that window. A zero count means no cards of that type in the window. It does not mean the calendar sync is healthy. Drift stays on `GET /cockpit/api/pipeline-health`.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "days": 7,
  "by_action": []
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/notifications

# Notifications

## What it does

Notifications are the in-app inbox, so a pending decision or a finished run reaches you without another channel.

Open **Notifications** (`/notifications`). The list is yours. Mark an item read or dismissed. Those are the two terminal states the screen writes. The inbox is per user. Another member's items are not in it.

The screen only calls the session API. Agents use the same two operations through MCP, scoped to the token owner.

## MCP tools

| Tool | Scope | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `cockpit_notifications_list` | `cockpit:read` | List. `status` defaults to `unread`. `limit` up to 100 |
| `cockpit_notification_resolve` | `cockpit:write` | Set `status` to `read` or `dismissed` |

`cockpit_get` (`cockpit:read`) includes notifications in the home aggregate. Use the list tool when you only want the inbox.

## HTTP endpoints

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/notifications` | Inbox for the signed-in user. Returns `unread` and `items` |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/notifications/:id` | Body `{ "status": "read" }` or `{ "status": "dismissed" }` |

## Permissions

Token scopes come from one permission-set layer: `cockpit:read` to list, `cockpit:write` to resolve. The screen uses the signed-in session and only returns that user's rows.

Row access is RLS by creator. Admins see all rows on shared CRM objects. This inbox stays the signed-in user's. An admin does not read another member's notifications through this screen.

## Agent example

Call `cockpit_notifications_list`, then resolve one id from that result.

```json
{
  "tool": "cockpit_notifications_list",
  "arguments": {
    "status": "unread",
    "limit": 20
  }
}
```

Expected result: unread items for the token owner. Resolving an id with `cockpit_notification_resolve` and `status` `read` removes it from the unread list. Resolving an id that belongs to someone else is rejected.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "notifications": [
    {
      "id": "notice-1",
      "status": "unread",
      "title": "Approval waiting"
    }
  ]
}
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/meetings

# Meetings and extraction

## What it does

Extraction is headless. There is no extraction screen. Review, thresholds, and metrics are API calls. The app is a thin client over the same approval rows and the same permission layer.

A proposal is an approval whose `item_type` is `extraction.<action_type>`. It uses the approvals queue. Quality-classification audits and decision-flow graphs are different objects. See [Decisions](/docs/features/decisions) and [Decision flows](/docs/features/decision-flows).

Adjacent screens read the same rows. They are not the review contract:

| Screen | What it shows |
|---|---|
| [Calendar](/docs/features/calendar) | Events. `/timeline` redirects here |
| [Activities](/docs/features/activities) | Ingested mail, calendar, meetings, and other activity |
| [Meeting pipeline](/docs/features/meeting-pipeline) | Health of the ingest lane |
| [KG Health](/docs/features/kg-health) | Counts and extraction gaps |
| [Approvals](/docs/features/approvals) | The queue where extraction proposals wait |

## MCP tools

| Tool | Scope | Inputs | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `extraction_pending` | `approvals:read` | `action_type` (optional), `limit` (default 20, max 100), `offset` (default 0) | Array of pending rows: `id`, `item_type`, `title`, `summary`, `proposed_payload`, `agent_irac`, `agent_skill_versions`, `created_at` |
| `extraction_review` | `approvals:write` | `approval_id`, `decision` (`approved` or `rejected`), `note` (optional) | `resolve_approval` object: `resolved`, `id`, `item_type`, `status`, `decided_by`, `decided_by_kind`, `human_only` |
| `extraction_review_bulk` | `approvals:write` | `action_type`, `decision`, `note` (optional), `limit` (default 20, max 100) | `{ ok, action_type, decision, updated, results }`. `updated` is how many ids were resolved |
| `extraction_threshold_set` | `approvals:write` | `action_type`, `threshold` (0 to 1) | `{ ok, action_type, threshold }` |
| `extraction_metrics` | `approvals:read` | `days` (default 30) | One object per action type: `pending`, `approved`, `rejected`, `agent_agreed`, `total_resolved`, `agreement_rate` |

Extraction is headless. These tools are the API. The screens above only show the rows the tools write.

`extraction_pending`, `extraction_review_bulk`, and `extraction_metrics` add `owner_user_id =` the caller when the token has an owner. They do not widen the list for an admin.

`action_type` on the list and bulk tools matches `item_type` exactly as `extraction.<action_type>`. Omit it on the list to return every pending `extraction.%` row.

`agreement_rate` is the share of resolved rows whose `agent_irac.recommendation` equals the final status, as a two-decimal string, or null when nothing is resolved.

`extraction_review` and `extraction_review_bulk` call `resolve_approval`. A user session records `auth.uid()` as human. A personal access token records the token as agent. Approve runs the card's `on_approve`. Reject applies nothing. A failed `extraction_apply` aborts the approve and leaves the card `pending`.

`approval_list` and `approval_resolve` are the general tools for the same table. Human-only types stay on a person. See [Approvals](/docs/features/approvals) and [Permissions and API keys](/docs/reference/permissions).

### What approve and reject do

| Decision | Effect |
|---|---|
| `rejected` | The approval leaves `pending`. Nothing is applied |
| `approved` | `on_approve` runs. Router cards use kind `extraction_apply` |

A router card stores `proposed_payload` `{ extraction, activity_id }` and `on_approve` `{ kind: "extraction_apply", action_type, activity_id, extraction }`. A `merge` item with winner, loser, and table uses kind `entity_merge` instead. Approving runs that payload. The direct-apply path below runs before a card exists, and only for two action types.

### Thresholds

Thresholds live in `extraction_thresholds`, one row per `action_type`, from 0 to 1. Lookup is the row for that action, then a row whose action is `*`, then `1.0`.

Seeded rows, all `1.0`: `mention_promote`, `new_record`, `enrich_fact`, `new_mention`.

A proposal auto-applies only when its confidence is greater than or equal to the threshold **and** the threshold is below `1.0`. A threshold of `1.0` queues every proposal of that type. Lower a threshold only for an action you trust.

`extraction_threshold_set` requires an admin in the database as well as `approvals:write`. A session must pass `is_admin()`. A `cbpat_` call must pass `is_admin_for` for the token owner. There is no chytr screen for editing thresholds.

### Action types

The activity pass emits these `action_type` values. Each queued card is `item_type` `extraction.<action_type>`. Approve applies them through `extraction_apply`. Direct apply, before a card exists, handles only two of them.

| `action_type` | On approve | Direct apply when the gate passes |
|---|---|---|
| `link` | Link the activity to an existing contact, account, deal, campaign, or project | Queued. The direct executor does not handle it |
| `enrich_fact` | Write one allow-listed field on an existing contact or account | Applied when the target exists and the field is allowed. Otherwise queued |
| `new_mention` | Ensure the contact or account, then insert a mention | Applied when that entity exists and the mention is new. Otherwise queued |
| `new_record` | Same apply as `new_mention`: find or create, then mention | Queued |
| `action_item` | Create a follow-up task | Queued |
| `quality_refine` | Set `activities.quality_class` | Queued |
| `deal_proposal` | Insert a deal when that owner has no deal of the same name | Queued |

`enrich_fact` may write, on contacts: `title`, `phone_primary`, `linkedin_url`, `lifecycle_stage`, `seniority`. On accounts: `industry`, `employee_count_range`, `annual_revenue_range`, `headquarters_city`, `headquarters_country`, `website`. `job_title` maps to `title`. `phone` maps to `phone_primary`.

Direct applies are written to `extraction_auto_apply_audit`. A repeat approve is a no-op when the row already matches. Apply failure leaves the card `pending`.

### How a proposal is filed

**Status.** Ingest does not call the router. The orchestrator sets extraction to not-run. The classifier writes `quality_class` and a `classifier` object onto `activities.extraction_result`. It does not insert `extraction.*` approvals.

A transcript can mint a workflow task. That task calls `extraction-route`, which calls the router. No transcript, or no stored extractions, skips the task. The review tools above operate on rows that already have type `extraction.%`.

When the router does run, each item becomes either a direct apply or a pending approval:

- `item_type`: `extraction.<action_type>`
- `status`: `pending`
- `proposed_payload`: `{ extraction, activity_id }`
- `on_approve`: `{ kind: "extraction_apply", ... }` (or `entity_merge` for a complete merge item)
- `owner_user_id`: the activity owner
- `requested_by`: `extraction-route`
- `assigned_to`: `human`

Activity quality classes are `substantive`, `transactional`, `notification`, `digest`, and `noise`. Digest and noise stop before extraction and stay out of the embedding index. Transactional rows are marked skipped for extraction.

### Meeting check-in

An agent files a meeting with `meeting_graph_checkin` (scope `graph:write`). Required input is `activity` with `type` `meeting_note` and `source_id`. Optional: `run_id`, `actor`, `work_item_id`, `entities`, `links`, `notes`, `flags`.

The call writes the activity, links, and notes, and returns a report with `run_id`, `activity_id`, `activity_inserted`, `applied_fields`, `flags_created`, `links_created`, `notes_created`, plus `lane`. Creates, and any update that touches identity fields, become pending approvals in that same call. A recognized auto-pass tier on a plain update applies immediately. `graph_checkin` is the deprecated alias and adds `deprecated: true` and `use_instead: meeting_graph_checkin`. `graph_checkin_revert` undoes one run by `run_id`.

`meeting_brief_checkin` (scope `graph:write`) attaches a pre-call brief to a calendar activity. It does not change entities. Required: `calendar_activity_id` and `brief`.

`activity_create` (scope `activities:write`) upserts a single activity when you are not sending a whole meeting.

### Identity rules on create cards

These apply when a create is filed through `approval_create` or a check-in flag, which is the path that still waits on a person:

- A contact whose name is a single token, with no email and no account, is stored with lifecycle stage `needs-review`.
- `prospect` on a lifecycle field is normalized to `lead`.
- `graph_entity_create` is human-only. An agent may file the card. `approval_resolve` will not approve it.

## HTTP endpoints

These routes use the signed-in session cookie. Responses are `{ "ok": true, ... }` or `{ "ok": false, "error": "..." }`. There is no `/extraction` resource.

| Method | Path | Body | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/approvals` | — | `{ ok, approvals }`. Pending rows, up to 500, every type. Filter `item_type` starting with `extraction.` |
| `GET` | `/cockpit/api/approvals/:id` | — | `{ ok, approval }`. Any status |
| `PATCH` | `/cockpit/api/approvals/:id` | `{ "status": "approved" \| "rejected", "note": "..." }` | `{ ok, id, status, updated }` where `updated` is the row count |
| `POST` | `/cockpit/api/approvals/bulk` | `{ "ids": ["..."], "status": "approved" \| "rejected", "note": "..." }` | `{ ok, updated, status }`. `ids` length 1 to 200 |

A session update records that user as human. Approve still runs `on_approve`. An update with no session user is refused. See [Approvals](/docs/features/approvals).

## Permissions

Token scopes come from one permission-set layer, as the table shows. `extraction_threshold_set` also requires an admin (`is_admin()` for a session, `is_admin_for` for a token). The screens use the signed-in session.

List, bulk review, and metrics stay on the caller's `owner_user_id`. They do not widen for an admin.

Approval rows use creator RLS: the row owner, `is_admin()`, or a token with the matching approvals scope. A workspace role is not `is_admin()`. Creator-only access on every CRM table is still the target. See [Row access](/docs/reference/permissions#row-access).

## Agent example

Call `extraction_pending` before you approve anything.

```json
{
  "tool": "extraction_pending",
  "arguments": {
    "action_type": "link",
    "limit": 10
  }
}
```

Expected result: an array of pending rows, or `[]`. `extraction_review` with `decision` `approved` runs that card's `on_approve` (`extraction_apply` on a router card). A failed apply leaves the card pending. `rejected` applies nothing.

```json
[
  {
    "item_type": "extraction.link",
    "title": "Link contact"
  }
]
```

# source: https://chytr.ai/docs/features/search

# Search

## What it does

Search answers two different questions: who has this name, and what did we write about them.

chytr has two searches. They answer different questions.

## Top bar
